speaker: READER
text: Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Why does the man who survived the flood end up drunk in his tent? What did Ham actually do? Why is Canaan cursed, when Ham did the wrong? And how was this chapter twisted to defend slavery? Four questions. Twelve verses.
ref: study.oneStory, study.hermeneutics.debates[0], study.hermeneutics.debates[1], study.hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription (the four questions are ours; each is answered from the study)

speaker: READER
text: The sons of Noah who came out of the ark were Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And Ham was the father of Canaan.

speaker: READER
text: These three were the sons of Noah, and from them the whole earth was populated.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Three names. And from them, the whole earth. Every people that will ever live is about to come from this one family. The next chapter will trace them, nation by nation.

speaker: GUIDE
text: But listen to the line the narrator adds before anything has happened. And Ham was the father of Canaan. He will say it again in a moment. Canaan plays no part in the scene. The narrator is telling us to watch him.

speaker: READER
text: Now Noah, a man of the soil, proceeded to plant a vineyard.

speaker: GUIDE
text: A man of the soil. In Hebrew, ish ha'adamah. A man of the ground. Adamah is the ground Adam was taken from. The ground that was cursed. When Noah was born, his father Lamech named him in hope of relief from

speaker: READER
text: the ground that the LORD has cursed

speaker: GUIDE
text: Now the ground gives its best gift. A vineyard.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The verb behind proceeded to is chalal. To begin. And in these chapters that verb keeps opening new beginnings that go wrong. Before the flood,

speaker: READER
text: when men began to multiply

speaker: GUIDE
text: After it, Nimrod

speaker: READER
text: began to be a mighty one

speaker: GUIDE
text: And at Babel,

speaker: GOD
text: if they have begun to do this

speaker: GUIDE
text: Every fresh start in the early world carries the seeds of new trouble.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Wine was for feasts and offerings across the ancient world. Scripture can praise

speaker: READER
text: wine that gladdens the heart of man

speaker: GUIDE
text: and it can warn that

speaker: READER
text: wine is a mocker

speaker: GUIDE
text: If Noah was the first to plant a vine, he may not have known what it could do. The text does not excuse him. And it does not lecture him either. It simply tells us what happened.

speaker: READER
text: But when he drank some of its wine, he became drunk and uncovered himself inside his tent.

speaker: GUIDE
text: So why does the righteous man end the story drunk in his tent? Because the flood had not solved the human problem. This is Noah who

speaker: READER
text: walked with God

speaker: GUIDE
text: Saved from judgment. Blessed with the words of creation. And within a few verses of the covenant, he falls into shame. The new world is not an innocent world.

speaker: GUIDE
text: God had said it before the rain had dried. He would never again destroy the earth,

speaker: GOD
text: even though every inclination of his heart is evil from his youth

speaker: GUIDE
text: The flood cleaned the world. It could not clean the heart.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Listen to the pattern. A man of the ground plants, as God planted a garden. The fruit is taken and consumed. Nakedness is exposed. Shame follows. A garment covers it. A knowing comes afterward. And the scene ends in curse and blessing.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The second father of humanity repeats the failure of the first. A new start from inside the old humanity, even one led by a righteous man, cannot make a clean world.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Uncovered himself. The verb is galah, to uncover, to expose, and here its form turns back on Noah. He is the one who exposed himself.

speaker: READER
text: And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers outside.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Nakedness. Ervah. It means more than an unclothed body. It carries shame and disgrace. And there is the narrator's second warning. Ham, the father of Canaan.

speaker: GUIDE
text: So what did Ham actually do? The text says only two things. He saw, and he told. Most readers through history have taken that plainly. The looking itself was the offence, and he made it worse by spreading it. In a culture of honour and shame, that was contempt for a father.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Others note that in Leviticus, seeing or uncovering nakedness is a way of speaking of a sexual act, and suggest something worse happened in that tent.

speaker: GUIDE
text: But the text says Noah uncovered himself, and the brothers put it right with a garment. That fits a sin of looking and exposing. Shameful, but no more than the words say. Either way, Ham dishonoured his father, and did it in the open.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The prophet Habakkuk links wine and exposure the same way. He pronounces woe on the one who gives his neighbours drink,

speaker: READER
text: in order to gaze at their nakedness

speaker: READER
text: Then Shem and Japheth took a garment and placed it across their shoulders, and walking backward, they covered their father’s nakedness. Their faces were turned away so that they did not see their father’s nakedness.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Watch how slowly the narrator tells it. Ham saw and told. Two verbs. His brothers took the garment, placed it, walked backward, covered their father, and did not see. Almost frame by frame. Their refusal to look stands out against his looking.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Three times in two verses, the narrator names the father's nakedness. And the garment has the article in Hebrew. The garment. As if one particular cloak was at hand. They covered him without a second look.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Ham exposes. His brothers cover. Ham tells. They act without a word. It is a lesson in how to treat someone else's failure.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The brick-maker heard the weight of this at Sinai. The fifth commandment.
ref: study.crossReferences[5] (the brick-maker is the series' first hearer)

speaker: GOD
text: Honor your father and mother

speaker: GUIDE
text: Israel's law made it a capital crime to strike or curse a parent, and Moses pronounced a curse on

speaker: READER
text: he who dishonors his father or mother

speaker: GUIDE
text: This was not only good manners. It reflects God's own order. The Son honours the Father.

speaker: GUIDE
text: What carries forward from this scene is clear. A warning against drunkenness. Paul writes,

speaker: READER
text: Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion

speaker: GUIDE
text: The command to honour parents. And the call to cover the failings of others, not to broadcast them. The New Testament puts it simply. Love covers a multitude of sins.
ref: study.hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription, study.basic.crossReferences (1 Peter 4:8, from the study's summary, not quoted as Scripture)

speaker: READER
text: When Noah awoke from his drunkenness and learned what his youngest son had done to him,

speaker: READER
text: he said, “Cursed be Canaan! A servant of servants shall he be to his brothers.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: These are the only words Noah ever speaks in Scripture. And they are a curse and a blessing.

speaker: GUIDE
text: A servant of servants. Ebed abadim. It is the Hebrew way of saying the most. Like holy of holies, the most holy place. Servant of servants means the lowest servant of all.

speaker: GUIDE
text: So why is Canaan cursed, when Ham did the wrong? Some see a correspondence. A son wronged his father, so he is struck through his son. Some suggest Canaan took part, though the text does not say so.

speaker: GUIDE
text: But the best answer is in the narrator's own signals. He flagged Canaan twice. The oracle is a prophecy. It looks ahead to the Canaanites Israel would meet, a people whose conduct would come to match their forefather's sin.

speaker: GUIDE
text: For the brick-maker, Canaan was not an idea. It was the land across the river. God warned Israel that its peoples had defiled the land, and that Israel held no immunity. If they copied Canaan, the land would cast them out too.
ref: study.crossReferences[2], study.context.historical (the brick-maker is the series' first hearer)

speaker: GUIDE
text: And the judgment did not come in haste. God told Abram

speaker: GOD
text: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete

speaker: GUIDE
text: The curse waited for centuries, until their own sin had filled up. Scripture insists that each person answers for their own sin.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Israel's first hearers saw the oracle at work in their own history. Canaanite towns were put to forced labour. The Gibeonites became

speaker: READER
text: woodcutters and water carriers

speaker: GUIDE
text: Now the fourth question. For centuries, some claimed a curse of Ham to justify the enslavement of Africans. It is one of the worst misuses of the Bible in history.

speaker: GUIDE
text: And the text gives it no ground. Read it again. Ham is not cursed. Canaan is. The Canaanites lived in the land between Egypt and Syria. And the sons of Ham usually linked with Africa, Cush, Mizraim and Put, are not cursed at all.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Noah's words are a prophecy of what would come of these lines. They are not a command to anyone to enslave anyone. And servant of servants is not a comment on the worth of any people before God.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Any reading that turns this oracle into a ranking of races abuses the text. Shem, Ham and Japheth were brothers. One family. And every nation on earth comes from them.

speaker: READER
text: He also declared: “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem! May Canaan be the servant of Shem.

speaker: READER
text: May God expand the territory of Japheth; may he dwell in the tents of Shem, and may Canaan be his servant.”

speaker: GUIDE
text: Listen to what Noah blesses. Not Shem. Blessed be the LORD, the God of Shem. Barak. To speak good over someone. The blessing lies in whom Shem has as his God.

speaker: GUIDE
text: And this is the only place in the oracle where the covenant name appears. The LORD. It is joined to Shem. For Japheth, Noah says simply, God.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Shem means name. In two chapters, the builders of Babel will say, let us

speaker: READER
text: make a name for ourselves

speaker: GUIDE
text: And God will say to Abram, Shem's descendant,

speaker: GOD
text: I will make your name great

speaker: GUIDE
text: The blessing of the God of Shem becomes the blessing of the God of Abraham.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Then Japheth. May God expand. In Hebrew, yapht. It sounds like his name, yepheth. Both names carry their future. Japheth will be enlarged. Shem will bear the name of God.

speaker: GUIDE
text: But who will dwell in the tents of Shem? Some read it as God Himself, making His presence live among Shem's descendants. Most translations read it as Japheth, coming to share in Shem's blessing.

speaker: GUIDE
text: The two are not far apart. If God dwells in Shem's tents, and Japheth comes to live there, both point to one hope. The nations joining the people among whom God has chosen to live.

speaker: READER
text: After the flood, Noah lived 350 years.

speaker: READER
text: So Noah lived a total of 950 years, and then he died.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Nine hundred and fifty years. And then he died. It is the refrain of Genesis five. Adam lived, and then he died. Noah's entry in that list began before the flood and was left open through the whole flood story. Now it is closed. The man who came through the waters still goes the way of Adam.

speaker: GUIDE
text: And notice what God does not do. The family He rescued fell into sin almost at once. And He sent no flood. His covenant faithfulness does not depend on ours.

speaker: GUIDE
text: God is sovereign over history. The oracle was spoken by a man who had failed, and it came to pass. God works through broken families to steer history toward His purpose.

speaker: GUIDE
text: Noah was set up as a second Adam. The father of a new humanity, blessed with Adam's words, a man of the ground. And like Adam, he fell. A new humanity needs a new head. Paul calls Christ

speaker: READER
text: the last Adam

speaker: GUIDE
text: Where Noah failed, and a son shamed his father, here is the faithful Son. Jesus said of His Father,

speaker: READER
text: I always do what pleases Him

speaker: GUIDE
text: Ham exposed his father's shame. Shem and Japheth covered it without looking. Christ went further than either. He did not look away from our shame. He took it on Himself. At the cross He was stripped, and soldiers divided His garments. He endured the cross,

speaker: READER
text: scorning its shame

speaker: GUIDE
text: so that the naked might be clothed. Paul writes,

speaker: READER
text: all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ

speaker: GUIDE
text: And the blessing on the God of Shem runs on. Shem's line goes to Abram, to Israel, to David. Luke traces Jesus back to

speaker: READER
text: the son of Shem, the son of Noah

speaker: GUIDE
text: The blessing announced in a tent after the flood reaches its goal in the one born in Bethlehem. And the tents? John says

speaker: READER
text: The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us

speaker: GUIDE
text: A word that recalls pitching a tent. And the Gentiles, the far nations, are brought in. Paul calls them

speaker: READER
text: no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints

speaker: GUIDE
text: And the curse? Christ

speaker: READER
text: redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us

speaker: GUIDE
text: In Christ there is no permanent class of the cursed. Rahab of Jericho, a Canaanite, was saved and became an ancestor of Christ. And a Canaanite woman once begged Jesus for her daughter. He praised her great faith and granted what she asked. Mercy, from the son of Shem, to the line of Canaan.

speaker: GUIDE
text: One care. The vineyard and the wine are not hidden pictures of the Lord's Supper. The links rest on the New Testament's own themes. The last Adam. The bearing of shame. The blessing of the nations.

speaker: GUIDE
text: At the end of the story, the people of God are dressed in white. The nations that came from Shem, Ham and Japheth are one family before the throne. And the curse that began with the ground is lifted.

speaker: READER
text: No longer will there be any curse

speaker: GUIDE
text: The brick-maker's father was old, and he had failed in his time, like every father. The story of Noah's sons taught Israel what kind of people to be. People who honour father and mother. People who cover shame instead of spreading it.
ref: study.hermeneutics.authorIntent (the brick-maker is the series' first hearer)

speaker: GUIDE
text: Ham exposed his father's shame. His brothers covered it. When you learn something embarrassing about someone, which brother are you more like?

speaker: GUIDE
text: Three sons. Three paths across the earth. Next, Genesis names their children, nation by nation. And every one of them is family.
ref: study.oneStory (series link to The Table of Nations, Genesis 10)
